spark.summary: Fault-tolerant replication protocols (Raft, Multi-Paxos, Quorum) that keep distributed state consistent across node crashes and network partitions using majority quorums (2f+1) and monotonic term numbers.
spark.keyTakeaway: Use Raft/Paxos quorums when you need linearizable state (locks, metadata, ledgers), and remember that even-numbered clusters add cost without improving fault tolerance.

concept.whyItMatters: Replicating data across servers is easy when nothing fails, but real networks drop packets, pause processes via GC, and split into partitions. Without a consensus protocol like Raft or Paxos, two nodes can simultaneously believe they are primary (split-brain), accepting conflicting writes and silently corrupting or losing committed transactions.
whenToUse: Control-plane metadata, distributed locks, and service discovery (etcd in Kubernetes, ZooKeeper, Consul) requiring strict linearizability.
Distributed transactional databases (CockroachDB, TiKV, YugabyteDB, Spanner) where Raft/Paxos groups replicate 64MB shards across availability zones.
Financial ledgers, inventory reservations, and sequence generators where stale reads or lost committed writes are unacceptable.
whenNotToUse: High-throughput caching, session stores, or social feeds where eventual consistency or asynchronous primary-replica replication suffices.
Cross-continental active-active writes where 150ms+ WAN round-trips for every synchronous quorum commit violate latency SLAs (unless using CRDTs or local-region homing).
Deploying a 2-node cluster expecting high availability—a 2-node quorum requires 2/2 nodes, actually *halving* availability on single-node failure.
keyPoints: Majority quorum (`floor(N/2) + 1`) guarantees any two quorums overlap by at least one node, preserving committed writes across leader elections: 3 nodes tolerate 1 failure, 5 nodes tolerate 2.

Raft decomposes consensus into Leader Election (monotonic `term` + `RequestVote`), Log Replication (`AppendEntries` with `prevLogIndex`/`prevLogTerm`), and Safety (only nodes with up-to-date logs can win election).
A write is only committed once replicated to a majority of nodes; the leader then advances `commitIndex` and applies it to the state machine.
Linearizable reads require either a quorum heartbeat round-trip (`ReadIndex`) or clock-bounded leader leases—reading blindly from a leader or follower risks stale reads during a partition.
Multi-Raft partitions keyspaces into thousands of small 64MB ranges so every node leads some ranges and follows others, scaling write throughput horizontally.

examples.title: Kubernetes Control Plane State in 5-Node etcd
examples.scenario: A production Kubernetes cluster spans 3 Availability Zones and must survive both a planned node upgrade and an unexpected AZ failure simultaneously.
examples.outcome: Running a 5-node etcd Raft cluster (`2f+1` with `f=2`) tolerates losing 2 nodes at once. During a rolling upgrade of Node 1, an unexpected crash of Node 2 still leaves 3/5 nodes healthy to form a quorum and serve linearizable pod-scheduling writes.

examples.title: Multi-Raft Leaseholder Reads in CockroachDB
examples.scenario: A global payments database stores account balances in 64MB Raft ranges replicated across 3 AZs (0.8ms RTT) and needs fast linearizable reads without a quorum round-trip on every `SELECT`.
examples.outcome: Each range elects a Raft Leaseholder with an exclusive time-bounded lease. The leaseholder serves strongly consistent reads locally in <1ms without contacting followers, falling back to quorum consensus only on writes or lease renewal.

tradeOffs.pro: 3 nodes minimize write replication fan-out and hardware cost while tolerating 1 failure.
tradeOffs.con: Zero margin during maintenance: if 1 node is down for patching, any second failure halts the entire cluster.

tradeOffs.pro: Zero data loss (RPO=0) on acknowledged writes and no split-brain divergence.
tradeOffs.con: Every write pays at least one network RTT to the closest quorum of followers (1–2ms intra-region, 80ms+ cross-region).

tradeOffs.pro: Single leader orders writes cleanly without vector clocks, sibling conflicts, or read-repair complexity.
tradeOffs.con: Write throughput for a single Raft group is bounded by one leader's CPU/network until sharded via Multi-Raft.

failureModes.name: Stale Leader Read (Split-Brain Illusion)
failureModes.description: A partitioned old leader does not yet know a new leader was elected in a higher term and serves stale data to clients hitting it directly.
failureModes.mitigation: Enforce `ReadIndex` (quorum heartbeat check before serving reads) or tightly bounded monotonic clock leases.

failureModes.name: Asymmetric Partition Election Storm
failureModes.description: A partially isolated follower cannot hear the leader's heartbeats, repeatedly increments its `term`, and disrupts the healthy cluster when packets occasionally leak through.
failureModes.mitigation: Enable Raft `Pre-Vote` extension so a node checks whether a majority would vote for it *before* incrementing its term.

failureModes.name: Even-Numbered Quorum Trap
failureModes.description: Deploying 2 or 4 nodes: a 2-node cluster has quorum=2 (0 fault tolerance), and a 4-node cluster has quorum=3 (same `f=1` tolerance as 3 nodes, at higher cost).
failureModes.mitigation: Always deploy odd node counts (3, 5, or 7) or add a lightweight non-data witness/arbiter node.

failureModes.name: Slow Disk `fsync` Stalling Quorum
failureModes.description: Consensus requires durable WAL `fsync` before acknowledging `AppendEntries`. Sharing etcd/Raft disks with noisy I/O neighbors spikes tail `fsync` latency, triggering false leader elections.
failureModes.mitigation: Dedicate local NVMe SSDs for the Raft WAL, monitor `wal_fsync_duration_seconds`, and tune `electionTimeout` (e.g., 10× heartbeat).

commonMistakes: Deploying a 2-node Raft/etcd cluster for HA, which actually lowers availability compared to a single node.
Reading from a Raft follower (`stale=true`) for authorization or inventory checks and assuming it is linearizable.
Stretching a single 3-node Raft cluster across 3 continents (US, EU, APAC) and wondering why every write takes 150ms+.
Setting `electionTimeout` too close to `heartbeatInterval` (e.g., 150ms vs 100ms) across noisy cloud networks, causing constant leadership flaps.
Putting large binary blobs (>1MB) into etcd/ZooKeeper, bloating Raft snapshots and stalling follower catch-up.

sections.content:
## The idea

Consensus protocols like **Paxos** and **Raft** solve a fundamental distributed systems problem: how can a cluster of unreliable machines agree on an ordered sequence of state transitions—and never lose a committed write—even when nodes crash or the network splits? The core mechanism is combining **monotonic term/ballot numbers** (fencing out stale leaders) with **intersecting majority quorums** (`floor(N/2) + 1`), guaranteeing that any newly elected leader's quorum overlaps with the quorum that committed prior writes.

## Concrete walkthrough

Trace a write `SET balance = 450` on a 3-node Raft cluster (Node A = Leader, Nodes B & C = Followers, `term = 4`):

1. **Append locally**: Client sends `SET balance = 450` to Leader A. A appends `(term=4, index=108)` to its durable WAL (`fsync`).
2. **Parallel `AppendEntries`**: Leader A sends `AppendEntries(term=4, prevLogIndex=107, prevLogTerm=4, entries=[108])` to B and C in parallel.
3. **Quorum Commit**: Node B verifies `prevLogIndex=107` matches its log, `fsync`s entry 108, and replies `success=true`. Even if Node C is slow or crashed, A + B form a majority (2 of 3). Leader A advances `commitIndex = 108`, applies `balance = 450` to its state machine, and returns `OK` to the client.
4. **Crash & Election**: Suppose Leader A now crashes permanently. Node B's `electionTimeout` (e.g., 1,000ms) fires. B increments to `term = 5` and sends `RequestVote(lastLogIndex=108, lastLogTerm=4)` to C. Because B's log is at least as up-to-date as C's, C grants its vote, B becomes Leader for `term = 5`, and `index=108` is guaranteed to survive.

sections.eyebrow: 03 / Paxos vs. Raft and linearizable read optimizations
sections.content:
## Paxos vs. Raft and linearizable read optimizations

While **Single-Decree Paxos** agrees on one value via `Prepare(n)/Promise` and `Accept(n, v)/Accepted`, real systems run **Multi-Paxos** (electing a stable leader to skip Phase 1 on steady-state writes). **Raft** is equivalent in safety and latency (1 RTT per committed write) but enforces contiguous log ordering and stricter election rules (a candidate must hold *all* committed entries to win, whereas Paxos allows out-of-order log holes that are reconciled later).

For **linearizable reads**, simply reading from the leader's memory is unsafe if the leader was partitioned and a new leader was elected. Systems solve this in two ways:
- **`ReadIndex` (etcd / TiKV)**: The leader records its current `commitIndex`, sends a lightweight heartbeat round to a majority to confirm it is still leader, waits until `appliedIndex >= ReadIndex`, and serves the read.
- **Leader Leases (CockroachDB / Spanner)**: Followers promise not to vote for any other candidate for `lease_duration` (e.g., 9s) using bounded clock-skew assumptions, allowing the leader to serve linearizable reads locally in 0 RTT.

## Replication & consensus model comparison

| Model | Fault Tolerance | Write Latency | Consistency Guarantee | Representative Systems |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Raft / Multi-Paxos** | `2f + 1` (tolerates `f` crashes) | 1 RTT to majority quorum | Linearizable (Strong) | etcd, CockroachDB, TiKV, Consul |
| **Async Primary-Replica** | Manual/automated failover (risks RPO>0) | 1 local write (0 quorum RTT) | Eventual on replicas | PostgreSQL async, MySQL async |
| **Leaderless Quorum (`R+W>N`)** | Survives `N - W` write failures | 1 RTT to `W` nodes | Tunable (requires read-repair/LWW for conflicts) | Apache Cassandra, DynamoDB (eventual/strong options) |
| **TrueTime / HLC + Paxos** | `2f + 1` per shard | 1 RTT + commit-wait (if clock skew) | External Consistency (Strict Serializability) | Google Spanner, CockroachDB (HLC) |

## Failure modes

- **Split-brain via un-fenced stale leader**: Serving reads without `ReadIndex` or valid leases lets an isolated ex-leader return stale balances.
- **Disk I/O starvation**: Sharing Raft WAL disks with application logs or container pulls spikes `fsync` latency past `electionTimeout`, causing cascading leader elections.
- **Snapshot transfer storms**: When a follower falls too far behind and its log is compacted, the leader streams a multi-gigabyte snapshot, saturating NIC bandwidth and triggering heartbeat timeouts.
- **Cross-region WAN latency**: Placing a 3-node quorum across US-East, EU-West, and AP-South forces every write to wait on a 150ms+ intercontinental RTT.

## Multi-Raft sharding and membership changes

A single Raft group serializes all writes through one leader's log. To scale horizontally, databases like CockroachDB and TiKV split data into 64MB–96MB key-range shards (**Multi-Raft**), running thousands of independent Raft state machines per node while coalescing heartbeats between node pairs.

When adding or removing nodes, **never change cluster membership from 3 to 5 directly in one jump**—two disjoint majorities could briefly form. Raft uses **Single-Server Membership Changes** (adding/removing 1 node at a time) or **Joint Consensus** (`C_old,new`) to guarantee majority overlap throughout the transition.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Always size consensus clusters to odd counts (3 for dev/standard HA, 5 for surviving simultaneous maintenance + node failure).
- [ ] Place nodes across 3 distinct failure domains (AZs or racks) within a single low-latency region (<5ms RTT) for OLTP quorums.
- [ ] Isolate Raft WAL storage on dedicated NVMe SSDs and monitor `wal_fsync_duration_seconds` p99 (<10ms).
- [ ] Enable `Pre-Vote` and `CheckQuorum` to prevent partitioned followers from disrupting healthy leaders.
- [ ] Use `ReadIndex` or clock-bounded leases for any read requiring linearizability; explicitly label follower reads as stale.
- [ ] Perform membership changes one node at a time and test single-node + AZ-loss failover regularly.

questions.title: Quorum Intersection Mathematical Guarantee
questions.prompt: In a distributed cluster of N=5 nodes, why does setting Read Quorum R=3 and Write Quorum W=3 guarantee strong consistency for all read queries?

options.text: Because 5 is a prime number.
options.explanation: Prime numbers are irrelevant to quorum intersection math.

options.text: Because R + W = 6 > 5 (N), ensuring at least one node in any read quorum set of 3 nodes overlaps with the latest write quorum set of 3 nodes.
options.explanation: Correct! Pigeonhole principle guarantees R + W > N sets intersect.

questions.sampleSolution: R + W (3 + 3 = 6) exceeds total nodes N=5. By the pigeonhole principle, any read quorum of 3 nodes must include at least one node from the write quorum.
questions.explanation: Set intersection math ensures stale reads are impossible when R + W > N.

interviewProblems.title: Global Multi-Region Distributed Key-Value Store
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: You are designing etcd for a global Kubernetes cluster spanning 5 cloud regions. During a cross-continent fiber cut, the cluster partitions into 2 nodes (Region A, B) and 3 nodes (Region C, D, E). How does your consensus protocol prevent split-brain data corruption?
constraints: Network partition isolates 2 nodes from 3 nodes.

dimensions.name: Majority Quorum Enforcement
dimensions.description: Requiring > N/2 (3 of 5) votes for Raft leader election and write commits.

dimensions.name: Minority Partition Behavior
dimensions.description: Rejecting writes on the 2-node minority partition.

interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Raft requires majority consensus (> N/2 = 3 nodes). The 3-node partition achieves majority (3/5), elects a leader, and accepts writes. The 2-node minority partition fails to reach quorum and steps down to read-only/error mode, preventing split-brain.
commonPitfalls: Allowing both sides of a network partition to accept writes.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Fault-tolerant replication protocols (Raft, Multi-Paxos, Quorum) that keep distributed state consistent across node crashes and network partitions using majority quorums (2f+1) and monotonic term numbers.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Node B (Follower) applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Node C (Follower).

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Node C (Follower) experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Enforce `ReadIndex` (quorum heartbeat check before serving reads) or tightly bounded monotonic clock leases.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Use Raft/Paxos quorums when you need linearizable state (locks, metadata, ledgers), and remember that even-numbered clusters add cost without improving fault tolerance.
Avoid trap: Deploying a 2-node Raft/etcd cluster for HA, which actually lowers availability compared to a single node.
Avoid trap: Reading from a Raft follower (`stale=true`) for authorization or inventory checks and assuming it is linearizable.
When to reach for it: Control-plane metadata, distributed locks, and service discovery (etcd in Kubernetes, ZooKeeper, Consul) requiring strict linearizability.
When to reach for it: Distributed transactional databases (CockroachDB, TiKV, YugabyteDB, Spanner) where Raft/Paxos groups replicate 64MB shards across availability zones.

putItTogether.title: Putting Consistency Replication Together
putItTogether.summary: Use Raft/Paxos quorums when you need linearizable state (locks, metadata, ledgers), and remember that even-numbered clusters add cost without improving fault tolerance.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Consistency Replication before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Running a 5-node etcd Raft cluster (`2f+1` with `f=2`) tolerates losing 2 nodes at once. During a rolling upgrade of Node 1, an unexpected crash of Node 2 still leaves 3/5 nodes healthy to form a quorum and serve linearizable pod-scheduling writes.
